summary: This chapter covers standard units of measurement, correct length measurement techniques, and different categories of motion. It introduces the International System of Units (SI unit) for length—the meter—and explains errors in length measurement such as parallax error and eye alignment. It further investigates states of rest versus motion, classifying motion into rectilinear (straight line), circular (rotational along a curved path), and periodic motion (repeating at regular time intervals).
topic_hierarchy: 5.1 Need for Standard Units - Non-standard handspans versus standard meter scale.
5.2 Correct Way to Measure Length - Scale placement and avoiding parallax error.
5.3 Measuring Length of Curved Lines - Thread method.
5.4 Rest vs. Motion - Defining reference points.
5.5 Types of Motion - Rectilinear, circular, and periodic motion.

glossary.definition: Motion of an object along a straight path.
glossary.example: An eraser falling vertically straight to the ground under gravity.

glossary.definition: Motion where an object moves along a circular path maintaining a fixed distance from a center point.
glossary.example: The motion of blades of an electric fan or hands of a clock.

glossary.definition: Motion that repeats itself at equal intervals of time.
glossary.example: The swinging bob of a pendulum or a child on a swing.

experiments_and_activities.aim: To classify moving objects around us and analyze rectilinear motion by dropping objects.
procedure: Observe 5 objects at rest and 5 in motion in classroom surroundings.
Drop an eraser from a height and observe its path.
experiments_and_activities.observations: The dropped eraser travels straight downwards in a line towards the floor.

side_boxes.content: Ancient non-standard units like cubits and handspans caused confusion because body sizes vary from person to person, leading to the creation of SI units.

misconceptions.error: An object can only undergo one type of motion at a time.
misconceptions.correction: Objects can exhibit multiple types of motion simultaneously; for instance, a rolling ball shows both rotational (circular) and rectilinear motion.

reasoning_qa.question: Why is a thread used to measure the length of a curved line instead of a rigid ruler?
reasoning_qa.answer: A flexible thread can closely trace the bends of a curved contour, after which the straightened thread is measured on a standard flat ruler.
